title: (Scenario) A service is healthy according to every dashboard — CPU, memory, pod count, request rate, aggregate error percentage all look normal — but customers report failures. How do you investigate (question what the dashboards are actually measuring — they may miss one tenant/region/endpoint/workflow/dependency path failing, because infrastructure health ≠ business-operation health) — and why must observability extend beyond infrastructure to customer-visible operations and business-level outcomes (a payment system returning HTTP 200 while failing to complete the intended business operation is not healthy)?
shortTitle: Every dashboard looks healthy but customers report failures — how do you investigate?

s1_definition.profdef: Infrastructure health and business-operation health are different things, and dashboards that measure only the former can show "all green" while customers are actively failing. Aggregate metrics — overall CPU, memory, pod count, total request rate, and a single blended error percentage — hide failures that are concentrated in one dimension: a single tenant, one region, one endpoint, one multi-step workflow, or one dependency path. A blended error rate of a fraction of a percent can completely mask one large customer failing one hundred percent of the time. Worse, a service can return HTTP 200 while failing to complete the business operation it was asked to perform, so even the error metric lies. The investigation technique is to question what the dashboards actually measure, disaggregate by every relevant dimension, and add observability for customer-visible operations and business outcomes rather than only infrastructure.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India head office looks at a wall of green dials: branches open, lights on, staff present, total footfall normal, overall complaint rate under one percent. Everything looks fine. But Priya, a large current-account holder, cannot complete a single transfer today, and so can nobody in the Mumbai branch using the international-transfer window. The green dials measured whether the building had power and how busy it was — not whether Priya's actual transfer completed. A teller stamping "received" on a form and then dropping it in the bin would also keep those dials green while silently failing every customer. The head office must measure whether real transactions actually finished, broken down by customer, branch, and transaction type — not just whether the lights are on.
s1_definition.oneliner: Green infrastructure dashboards prove the building has power, not that the customer's transaction completed — so measure business outcomes, disaggregated by tenant, region, endpoint, and workflow.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the payments platform serves many corporate tenants. The operations dashboard shows CPU, memory, pod count, total request rate, and one blended error percentage, all green. Yet Priya's company, a large tenant, reports that every one of their international transfers is failing.

Problem 1 — the blended error rate hides the failure. Priya's tenant is a small fraction of total traffic, so even at one hundred percent failure for her, the overall error rate barely moves and stays green. The dashboard genuinely cannot see her.

Problem 2 — the success metric is the HTTP status, not the business outcome. The international-transfer endpoint accepts the request and returns 200 after enqueuing, but the downstream FX settlement silently fails for Priya's corridor, so the money never moves while the dashboard counts a success.

The investigation disaggregates the error rate by tenant, region, and endpoint to surface that Priya's international-transfer endpoint is at one hundred percent failure, and adds a business-outcome metric that measures whether the transfer actually settled, not whether it returned 200. The mini-project builds a `MetricsStore` that records both aggregate and per-dimension outcomes, a `PaymentEndpoint` that returns 200 but silently fails settlement for one corridor, and an `Investigator` that disaggregates to find the hidden failure and compares HTTP success against business success.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: ten thousand operations. Nine thousand nine hundred fifty are healthy domestic transfers from many small tenants in Delhi. Fifty are Priya's company's international transfers from Mumbai, which return 200 but silently fail to settle.

Step 1 — Requests are recorded. Every operation returns HTTP 200, so the endpoint records a 200 for all ten thousand. For the fifty Mumbai international transfers, the business outcome is recorded as not settled, even though the HTTP status is 200.

Step 2 — The aggregate view. The investigator computes the blended HTTP 5xx error rate. Since everything returned 200, this is zero percent. The dashboard is perfectly green. Nothing here reveals Priya's problem.

Step 3 — Disaggregate by tenant. The investigator slices the business-failure rate per tenant. Every small tenant is at zero percent. PriyaCorp is at one hundred percent. This single slice exposes the failure that the aggregate completely hid.

Step 4 — The HTTP 200 lie. The investigator counts responses that returned 200 but did not complete the business operation. It finds fifty — exactly Priya's transfers. This proves the error metric itself was lying, because the customer saw "success" while the money never moved.

Step 5 — Conclusion. Infrastructure and aggregate error dashboards were green because they measured reachability, not correctness. Only disaggregation by tenant plus a business-outcome metric revealed that PriyaCorp's Mumbai international transfers were totally broken.

```
2026-10-24 18:45:33 [INFO] Aggregate HTTP 5xx error rate = 0.00% (dashboard looks green)
2026-10-24 18:45:33 [SEVERE] HIDDEN FAILURE: tenant PriyaCorp business-failure 100% (invisible in aggregate)
2026-10-24 18:45:33 [SEVERE] 50 requests returned HTTP 200 but FAILED the business operation
```

```
    ├─ 9,950 small-tenant domestic (Delhi) → settled
    └─ 50 PriyaCorp international (Mumbai) → HTTP 200 but settlement

  MetricsStore records (tenant, region, endpoint, httpStatus, businessOk)
    │
    ├─ Aggregate HTTP 5xx error = 0.00%  → DASHBOARD GREEN (lies)

  Alert: tenant failure > 20% AND reconciliation mismatch > 0 → page on-call
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When every dashboard is green but customers are reporting failures, my starting assumption is that the dashboards are measuring infrastructure health, not business health, and those are genuinely different things. CPU, memory, pod count, request rate, and a single blended error percentage all tell me the machines are alive and traffic is flowing. None of them tells me whether a specific customer's specific operation actually completed. So the first move in the investigation is to stop trusting the green and to ask precisely what each metric measures and what it could be hiding.

The most common hiding place is aggregation. If one large tenant sending a small slice of total traffic is failing one hundred percent, the blended error rate barely moves and the dashboard stays green while that customer is completely down. The same masking happens along any dimension — one region behind a bad config, one endpoint with a broken deploy, one step of a multi-step workflow, or one dependency path timing out while the others are fine. So I disaggregate: I slice error rate and latency by tenant, by region, by endpoint, by version, by dependency, and by workflow step, looking for any slice that is anomalous even when the whole is calm. That requires high-cardinality dimensioned metrics and structured logs with correlation IDs so I can ask, and answer, "what is the success rate for this tenant's international-transfer endpoint in this region right now."

The deeper and more dangerous issue is what I call the HTTP 200 lie. A service can return a success status while failing the business operation it was asked to perform. A payment endpoint can accept the request, return 200, enqueue the work, and then have the downstream settlement silently fail — the customer sees success, but the money never moves, and the error dashboard counts it as a win. In my banking work this is exactly the shape the problem took: a large corporate tenant's international transfers from one region returned 200 but never settled, and the blended error rate stayed at zero. We only found it by disaggregating by tenant and by adding a business-outcome metric that measured whether the transfer actually settled, not whether it returned 200.

So the principle I carry is that infrastructure health is necessary but not sufficient, and a mature observability stack has three layers: infrastructure metrics, request-level metrics disaggregated by every meaningful dimension, and business-outcome metrics tied to what the customer actually wanted — did the transfer settle, did the funds arrive, did the statement generate — backed by reconciliation jobs that compare intended versus actual state and synthetic transactions that run a real end-to-end operation and verify the final result. A payment system returning HTTP 200 while failing to complete the intended operation is not healthy, and if my dashboards can't tell the difference, then my dashboards, not my customers, are the thing that is broken.

---

keyPoints: Distributed tracing: Zipkin/Jaeger — follow request across services
Centralized logging: ELK/Loki — aggregate logs from all services
Metrics: Prometheus + Grafana — latency, error rate, throughput
Health checks and alerting: detect issues before users do
